title: How I structure the first five minutes of a coding interview
body:
Most of my early mistakes were not about algorithms. I started typing before I understood the problem.

What works for me now:

1. **Restate** the problem in one sentence.
2. **Ask** about input size, duplicates, negative values and empty input.
3. **Walk through** one small example by hand.
4. **Say the brute force** out loud, with its complexity, before improving it.
5. **Agree on the plan** with the interviewer, then code.

It feels slow, but interviewers consistently react better to a clear plan than to fast typing.

title: Two pointers vs sliding window: how do you decide?
body:
I keep mixing these up. My current rule of thumb:

- **Two pointers** when the array is sorted (or can be sorted) and you compare values at both ends.
- **Sliding window** when you need a contiguous range that satisfies a condition and the window can grow or shrink.

```python
left = 0
for right in range(len(a)):
    add(a[right])
    while not valid():
        remove(a[left]); left += 1
    best = max(best, right - left + 1)
```

Do you have a different mental model? Curious how others tell them apart.

title: Study plan for 8 weeks: what actually worked for me
body:
I had 8 weeks before placement season and about 2 hours a day.

**Weeks 1-2:** arrays, strings, hashing.
**Weeks 3-4:** two pointers, binary search, stacks.
**Weeks 5-6:** recursion, trees, basic DP.
**Week 7:** mixed timed sets, 3 problems in 60 minutes.
**Week 8:** revision of my own wrong submissions only.

The biggest gain came from re-solving problems I had failed, not from solving new ones.

title: First weekly contest: what I learned
body:
I finished only 1 of 4 problems in my first contest. Notes for other beginners:

- Read all problems first and start with the easiest, not the first.
- If a problem takes more than 20 minutes with no progress, move on.
- Test your own edge cases before submitting. Wrong attempts cost time.

I will try again this weekend and aim for two.

title: Switching from a non-CS branch to software: is it realistic?
body:
I am in my final year of a mechanical engineering degree and want to move into software.

So far I have finished a Python course, around 120 practice problems and one small web project. Is it realistic to target service-company roles first and move to product companies later?

Any advice on which projects to show would help.

title: Explaining your approach out loud: tips that helped me
body:
Silence in an interview is stressful for both sides. A few habits:

- Narrate what you are *considering*, not every keystroke.
- Name the data structure and why you chose it.
- When stuck, say what you tried and why it failed. That is useful signal for the interviewer.

Practice by recording yourself solving one problem a day. It is awkward at first, then very helpful.

title: Dynamic programming: a checklist that made it click
body:
When a problem asks for a count, a minimum, a maximum or a yes/no over choices, I run this checklist:

1. What is the **state**? (index, remaining capacity, last choice)
2. What are the **transitions**?
3. What is the **base case**?
4. Can I write the recursion first, then add memoization?
5. Can the table be shrunk to one row?

Writing the recursion first removed most of my fear of DP.

title: How do you balance college work and daily practice?
body:
My semester is heavy and I keep skipping practice. I tried a fixed two-hour block, but it breaks whenever there is a lab or an assignment.

What is working for people here: a small daily minimum (one problem), or longer sessions on weekends?

title: How to think about an offer beyond the headline number
body:
Some questions worth asking before comparing offers:

- How much is **fixed** and how much is variable or stock?
- Is there a **joining bonus** and is it paid back if you leave early?
- What is the **notice period** and the bond, if any?
- What does the **growth path** look like in the first two years?

The number matters, but these details can change the real value a lot.

title: Time management in a 90-minute contest
body:
What I try now:

- 0-5 min: skim every problem.
- 5-30 min: solve the easy one, double check, submit.
- 30-70 min: attempt the medium problem.
- Last 20 min: partial progress on the hard one, or re-check earlier answers.

How do you split your time?

title: Resume tips for freshers with no internship
body:
What recruiters at campus drives seem to look for:

- One page, clean layout, no photo.
- 2 or 3 projects with a **one-line outcome** each (what it does, what stack, any numbers).
- Coding profile links that open correctly.
- Skills section limited to what you can discuss for 10 minutes.

Remove anything you cannot explain in an interview.

title: How I prepare for the HR round
body:
Technical rounds get most of the attention, but the HR round eliminates people too.

Prepare short, honest answers for:
- Tell me about yourself (60 seconds, ends with why this role)
- A project you are proud of and your exact part in it
- A time you disagreed with a teammate
- Why this company

Write them down, then say them aloud. Do not memorize word for word.

title: Do you read editorial solutions before or after struggling?
body:
My rule is 30 minutes of honest attempt, then read only the **hint** or the first idea of the editorial, then close it and code on my own.

Reading the full solution immediately feels productive but I forget it within a week. What is your rule?

title: Understanding in-hand salary versus CTC
body:
A quick breakdown for freshers:

- **CTC** includes employer contributions, insurance and variable pay.
- **In-hand** is what reaches your account after PF, tax and deductions.
- Variable pay is usually not guaranteed every month.

Ask HR for the monthly in-hand estimate and the variable pay policy in writing before you decide.

title: Graphs: a short pattern list
body:
Most graph interview questions reduce to a few patterns:

- **BFS** for shortest path in an unweighted graph or grid.
- **DFS** for connected components, cycle checks, flood fill.
- **Union-Find** for dynamic connectivity.
- **Topological sort** for ordering with dependencies.
- **Dijkstra** for non-negative weighted shortest path.

Learn to spot which one the statement is hiding.

title: Is it worth doing a second language for backend roles?
body:

Would you invest time in learning a second stack, or go deeper into system design and databases first?

title: Small wins thread: share what you solved this week
body:
Let's keep this encouraging. Share one thing you solved or understood this week, however small.

Mine: I finally understood why a monotonic stack gives the next greater element in linear time. Each element is pushed and popped at most once.

title: Mock interviews with a friend: a simple format
body:
We run a 45-minute mock once a week and swap roles.

- 5 min: introductions and the problem statement
- 30 min: solve and discuss
- 10 min: written feedback on communication, correctness and edge cases

The feedback step is the valuable part. Be specific: *"you never checked an empty array"* is better than *"be more careful"*.
